passage:
In their Vancouver apartment, Bao turned the handle of the old tin box, playing a tinkly tune. Pop! A clown sprang out.
Xin gasped, eyes huge, and jerked back.
Bao pushed the clown back in and shut the lid. Xin frowned at the box, then looked up at her grandfather, puzzled.
“He's hiding inside,” Bao said. “Turn the handle, and he jumps out.”
Xin put her hand on the handle. Bao helped her turn it.

qa.q: What sprang out of the old tin box?
qa.a: A clown sprang out.

qa.q: What was Xin feeling when she frowned at the closed box and looked at Bao?
qa.a: She was confused about where the clown had gone, after being surprised when it popped out, and looked to her grandfather to make sense of it.

qa.q: What did Bao do that helped Xin?
qa.a: He gave a short, simple explanation and let her turn the handle herself, which turned surprise and confusion into understanding.

qa.q: How might Bao feel when Xin reaches for the handle?
qa.a: He probably feels pleased and amused that she is curious rather than scared.

grounding: It shows a toddler gasping wide-eyed in surprise and frowning in confusion, with an adult giving reassurance and a short explanation.

passage:
I'm Lalit from next door. Nandini has one word at the moment, and it's “No!” With a big head shake.
Shoes? “No!” Bath? “No!” Last week her mother asked, “Banana?” — and Nandini shook her head hard and said “No!” while reaching for the banana.
Her mother didn't argue. She held up two fruits. “Banana or apple?”
Nandini thought about it, pointed at the banana, and nodded. She looked very pleased with herself.

qa.q: What did Nandini reach for while saying "No"?
qa.a: She reached for the banana.

qa.q: Why did Nandini say "No!" to a banana she wanted?
qa.a: She seemed to enjoy the feeling of control that saying no gives her, rather than truly opposing the banana; her pleased look after choosing shows she liked having a say.

qa.q: What did Nandini's mother do that worked?
qa.a: She offered a limited choice, "Banana or apple?", which let Nandini feel in charge without a battle.

qa.q: How does Lalit see Nandini's constant "No!"?
qa.a: Lalit finds it amusing and notices that her no doesn't always mean she doesn't want the thing.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler shaking her head and saying no for a sense of control, and an adult offering a limited choice to honour her autonomy.

passage:
Daycare note, Monday. From Irfan, room teacher.
At lunch Ishita pointed at the pot and said, “More!” I said, “More rice,” and gave her some.
Later she tried to climb the slide, slipped onto her bottom and didn't cry. She just reached both arms up to me, bottom lip out.
I said, “You want up. You got a fright,” and picked her up. She held on for a long time.
The same reaching can mean “give me” or “hold me."

qa.q: What did Ishita point at during lunch?
qa.a: She pointed at the pot.

qa.q: What did Ishita want when she reached up after slipping?
qa.a: She wanted comfort and to be held because she had a fright, even though she did not cry; her pushed-out lip showed she was upset.

qa.q: How did Irfan respond well to both of Ishita's requests?
qa.a: Irfan named each request in words, "More rice" and "You want up," and answered it, noticing that the second was a need for comfort.

qa.q: What would change if Irfan had treated the reach after the slide as nothing?
qa.a: Ishita might have been left upset and alone with her fright, and learnt that her signals are not answered.

grounding: It shows a toddler reaching and pointing to request food and to be picked up, with the adult naming the request and noticing the need for comfort.

passage:
Smoke curled from the clay chulha in the corner of the village kitchen. Yogesh toddled straight towards it, hand out.
“NO! Hot!” Kalyani's voice rang out sharp.
Yogesh froze and stared at her, lip trembling.
She was already there, scooping him up and stepping back. “Hot. Ouch,” she said, touching his hand. Then she dragged the wooden plank across the corner so he couldn't reach it.
Yogesh stared at the fire, then buried his face in her neck.

qa.q: What did Kalyani drag across the corner?
qa.a: She dragged the wooden plank across the corner.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he froze at Kalyani's sharp "NO!"?
qa.a: He was startled and a little frightened, reading the sharp voice as a sign of danger, which stopped him.

qa.q: Which choices kept Yogesh safe, and why?
qa.a: A short, sharp warning, lifting him away at once and putting the plank across the corner; simple words and physical safety matter more than a long explanation at his age.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel after the moment passes?
qa.a: She probably feels shaken and relieved that she stopped him in time.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler responding to a sharp no as a danger signal, with the adult using short words and a physical barrier to keep him safe.

subtype: Refusing with no and pulling away [Expressing]
passage:
I'm Chetan, and my little sister Shreya is two. When Mama's friend visited, he bent down to pinch her cheek.
Shreya turned her face away and pushed his hand with both of hers. “No!”
“Arre, just a small pinch,” he said.
Mummy said, “She doesn't want it, and that's okay. Maybe a high five?” Shreya held up her hand.
At dinner she pushed her bowl away. “No more.” Mummy took the bowl away.

qa.q: How old is Shreya?
qa.a: Shreya is two.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she turned away and pushed the hand?
qa.a: She was uncomfortable with the cheek pinch and did not want to be touched, and her push and "No!" clearly said so.

qa.q: Why was Mummy right to back Shreya's "No"?
qa.a: Respecting her small refusals about touch and food, where it is safe, teaches Shreya that her body belongs to her.

qa.q: How did Mama's friend react to Shreya pushing his hand?
qa.a: He seemed to brush it off, saying it was just a small pinch.

grounding: It shows a toddler refusing touch and food by saying no and pushing away, and an adult respecting those refusals.

passage:
Playgroup note, Thursday. From Tushar, helper.
At snack time Pradeep held out his half-eaten biscuit to me, soggy, with a big smile. I said, “For me? Thank you!” and pretended to munch. He laughed.
Later he pushed his toy car into another child's hands, all by himself.
A few minutes later he wanted it back and cried. I didn't make him share; I helped the other child find a truck.

qa.q: What did Pradeep hold out at snack time?
qa.a: His half-eaten biscuit.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he offered his biscuit?
qa.a: He seemed happy and friendly, sharing on the spur of the moment to connect with Tushar; the big smile shows it was a pleasure to give.

qa.q: Why did Tushar not make Pradeep share the car again?
qa.a: Forcing sharing would take the joy out of it; warmly thanking his spontaneous offers encourages kindness better.

qa.q: How might the other child have felt when Pradeep gave the car?
qa.a: The other child was probably surprised and pleased, and then disappointed when Pradeep wanted it back.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler spontaneously offering food and a toy, and an adult responding warmly without forcing sharing.

passage:
I'm Rehana. I was pushing my baby brother on the swing when I saw Deepika at the sandpit.
Another little girl had fallen and was crying loudly. Deepika toddled over, stared at her, then patted her back, pat, pat, pat.
Then she ran off, came back with her own teddy and pushed it into the girl's arms.
Deepika's mother knelt down. “That was kind, Deepika. You helped her feel better.”
Deepika beamed.

qa.q: What did Deepika bring the crying girl?
qa.a: She came back with her own teddy.

qa.q: What does Deepika's patting and bringing her teddy suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt concern for the crying girl and wanted to help her feel better, an early sign of care.

qa.q: How did Deepika's mother support her kindness?
qa.a: She noticed it warmly and named it, "That was kind," which encourages Deepika to care for others.

qa.q: How might the girl who fell have felt when Deepika patted her?
qa.a: She may have felt comforted and less alone.

grounding: It shows a toddler patting a crying child and bringing a toy to comfort her, an early sign of empathy noticed warmly by an adult.

passage:
At the family gathering in the small town, Saurabh clung to Anjali all afternoon, cuddled on her lap, reaching up whenever she stood.
Then his Bua swept in. “Give me a kissy, Saurabh!” She leaned in.
Saurabh turned his face away and pressed into Anjali's shoulder.
“He doesn't want to right now, Didi,” said Anjali. “Maybe a wave?”
Bua's face fell for a second, then she laughed. Saurabh gave her a tiny wave from his mother's arms.

qa.q: Who swept in and asked for a kiss?
qa.a: His Bua swept in and asked for a kissy.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when he turned away from his Bua's kiss?
qa.a: He felt shy and unsure in the busy gathering, wanting to stay close to his mother, and did not want to be kissed right then.

qa.q: Why was Anjali's answer a wise one?
qa.a: It respected Saurabh's right to refuse a kiss while offering a friendly wave instead, which kept things warm with Bua.

qa.q: How did Bua feel when Saurabh turned away?
qa.a: Her face fell for a second, showing she was a little hurt, but she laughed it off.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler cuddling and seeking his mother, and an adult respecting his right to refuse a relative's kiss.

passage:
From Irfan Mamu's notebook, Himani's second birthday.
When I gave Himani the drum, her mother said, “What do we say?” Himani hugged the drum and said, “Tank oo,” then banged it hard, grinning.
Later she handed her Nani a toy duck and waited. Nani said, “Thank you!” and Himani clapped.
I don't think she knows what thanks means yet. But she knows the drum made her happy, and that pleased her.

qa.q: What did Irfan Mamu give Himani?
qa.a: He gave Himani the drum.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she hugged the drum and said "Tank oo"?
qa.a: She was delighted with the drum; the words were prompted and copied, but the pleasure was real.

qa.q: How can adults help Himani grow real gratitude over time?
qa.a: Keep modelling "thank you" warmly, as Nani did, without pressure, so the words gradually join the good feeling.

qa.q: What was it like for Nani to receive the toy duck?
qa.a: Nani seemed pleased and played along with a warm "Thank you!", which made Himani clap.

grounding: It shows a toddler giving a prompted thank-you and a hug after a gift, carrying real pleasure before a grasp of gratitude.

passage:
The power went out in the Bengaluru flat with a click, and the room went black. Kashish screamed.
Jeevan grabbed her up fast, jiggling her hard. “Shh, shh, shh!” She screamed louder.
He stopped. Took a breath. Then he sat on the bed, held her against his chest and rocked slowly, his voice low. “Dark. Papa's here. Dark.” He stroked her back, slow and steady.
Her screams turned to sniffs. Soon she was quiet against him.

qa.q: What did Jeevan say in a low voice?
qa.a: "Dark. Papa's here. Dark."

qa.q: Why did Kashish calm down after Jeevan changed how he held her?
qa.a: She felt safe once his voice was slow and low and his rocking gentle, even though she did not understand the words; the fast jiggling had felt tense and frightening.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Grabbing and jiggling her hard added to her fear; slowing down, sitting, rocking gently and speaking low calmed her.

qa.q: How did Jeevan likely feel when Kashish screamed louder?
qa.a: He likely felt alarmed and flustered, which is why he stopped and took a breath.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler calming to a slow, low voice, rocking and gentle touch, and tense handling making her more upset.
